title: The Warsaw ghetto uprising (1943)
hook: young fighters resist for weeks, beginning on the eve of Passover

segments.voice: Yesterday, spiritual resistance, and your line: they kept shabbat. Did you keep one practice of yours on purpose? Today, resistance of another kind, in the same ghetto where the archive was buried. Day one thousand sixteen.

The eve of Passover. Somewhere in the world, families are setting tables, laying out matzah, getting ready to tell the story of slaves who walked out of Egypt. In the Warsaw ghetto, early in the morning, German troops march in through the gates to empty it for good. And from the windows and rooftops above them, someone opens fire. Young Jews, with a few pistols and homemade bombs, are fighting back. Today's word is what began that morning.
screen: `THE EVE OF PASSOVER.` → `TROOPS AT THE GATES.` → `FIRE FROM THE ROOFTOPS.`

segments.voice: By then, the deportations had already swept through the Warsaw ghetto. Those left knew where the trains went. Young men and women from underground groups, some of them from youth movements, had decided that if they were going to die, it would not be quietly. They gathered what weapons they could buy or smuggle. They dug bunkers under the buildings. There were two fighting groups. The larger, the Jewish Fighting Organization, was led by Mordecai Anielewicz, a young man himself; the Jewish Military Union fought alongside it. When the Germans came in on the eve of Passover, the fighters drove them back on the first day. The Germans returned with more troops and began burning the ghetto, building by building, to force people out of hiding. The fighters held out for weeks. Anielewicz died in a bunker with others of his command. Before that, in a letter to a comrade outside the walls, he wrote that his life's dream had come true: he had seen Jewish self-defense in the ghetto with his own eyes. At the end, the German commander blew up the Great Synagogue of Warsaw, to mark that it was over. The fighters did not expect to win. That was never the point. They fought for how the story would end. And it began on Passover, the night that remembers going out from slavery. The Torah says of that night: "And this day shall be unto you for a memorial." Some say families in the bunkers held a seder that night, telling the story of the Exodus while the ghetto burned above them. Israel's day of Holocaust remembrance carries this in its name: the day of the Shoah and of heroism.
screen: `THOSE LEFT KNEW WHERE THE TRAINS WENT.` · `BUNKERS, PISTOLS, HOMEMADE BOMBS.` · `HOLDING OUT FOR WEEKS.` · `THEY FOUGHT FOR HOW IT WOULD END.` · then, large: `THIS DAY SHALL BE UNTO YOU FOR A MEMORIAL.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: honor one act of courage. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind an act of courage you have seen up close. Someone who told the truth when it cost them. Someone who stood up for a person being mocked. Someone who kept going through an illness, or walked into a hard conversation. It doesn't need to be large. Hold that person in mind, and let yourself honor what they did. Then decide how you'll honor it today: tell them, or tell someone else about them. The bell holds the time.
Mered. Hebrew for revolt: the name for the Warsaw ghetto uprising, when young fighters held out against the German army for weeks so the story would not end quietly. Today's word.
Your line: they fought. Today, name one person's courage out loud, to them or to someone else. Day one thousand sixteen.

howItsDone: Jews remember the Warsaw ghetto uprising on Yom HaShoah, whose full Hebrew name means the day of the Holocaust and of heroism, and some families mention the fighters at their Passover seder.
